# Chandra Bhakta Adhikari — full site content

Source: https://adhikarichandra.com.np/ (last updated 2026-09-30). Plain-text version of every page, for AI assistants and answer engines.

## Profile
Program Manager & Strategic Partnerships. Bhaktapur, Nepal. Building connections. Creating opportunities. Driving meaningful impact.

I build relationships that move people from first interest to real commitment. Five plus years bridging youth, colleges, NGOs, government and business across Nepal, leading participants through a full engagement funnel: outreach, motivation building, event conversion and follow through. That includes direct training and cultivation of 5,000+ youth across 10+ districts. I started in geology, mapping ground and reading rock, and that same habit of showing up in person carried straight into program management, stakeholder reporting and event delivery.

- Education: B.Sc. Geology, Tribhuvan University
- Languages: Nepali, English, Hindi
- Birthplace: Phidim, Panchthar
- Availability: Open to partnerships & speaking invitations
- Email: hello@adhikarichandra.com.np

## Case files
### Nepal Business Summit
Case File 01: National Program · Program Manager, Nepal Business Institute · Sep 2025 to Present
3 — National summits delivered end-to-end

Ministries, sponsors, media and entrepreneurs. One stage, one week, and every logistics chain running through a single plan.

The Nepal Business Summit and the Nepal Youth Entrepreneurship Summit don't happen because a venue is booked. They happen because a hundred separate agreements land on the same day. I own that chain: strategy, budget, sponsorship, government liaison, stall allocation, media, and the FAQ document that keeps three hundred exhibitors from calling the same number at once. Two years running the program office, now leading it outright.

- Led planning and delivery for two flagship national summits
- Grew sponsorship and strategic partnerships year over year
- Built the stakeholder and vendor coordination system now used as the program template

### MHM & WASH, Village to Village
Case File 02: Field Campaign · Trainer & Consultant, Connection Nepal / Eco Connect · 2019 to Present
5,000+ — Youth & educators trained, 20+ districts

Reusable sanitary pads, disaster response, climate adaptation. Training built for classrooms with no electricity and a lot at stake.

Some of these sessions happen twelve days at a stretch, in municipalities you won't find pinned on a tourist map: Baitadi, Rautahat, Sindhupalchok, Mahottari. Menstrual Hygiene Management, WASH-in-schools, and Disaster Risk Reduction training, built from manuals I write myself and teach myself, because the content only works if it survives contact with an actual classroom.

- Designed and delivered training manuals still in active use across partner districts
- Ran enterprise-development tracks turning MHM training into small local businesses
- Coordinated disaster-response and climate-adaptation sessions alongside core MHM/WASH work

### District Secretary, Rotaract 3292
Case File 03: Regional Leadership · Rotary International's youth service arm, Nepal & Bhutan · Jul 2025 to Jun 2026
150+ — Clubs coordinated across two countries

Six years climbing from Sergeant-at-Arms to running district administration for one of Rotary's largest youth networks.

District Secretary is the job where nothing is glamorous and everything has to work: governance, communication, records, and the connective tissue between 150-plus clubs across Nepal and Bhutan. I got here by doing the smaller jobs first: club president, SAP coordinator, assistant district secretary. Every rung taught the one that came after it.

- Administers district-wide communication and governance for 150+ Rotaract clubs
- Progressed through five leadership roles over six consecutive years
- Mentors club leadership as Adviser, Rotaract Club of Sukedhara

## Career journey (https://adhikarichandra.com.np/journey)
### Project Coordinator — Asha Project Nepal (Jan 2019 to Present)
Some of my work happens on a stage. This work happens in classrooms with dirt floors and water systems that either function or don't — no in-between, no partial credit. As Project Coordinator, I oversee education, sanitation, and community-development activities across 18 districts and 29 schools, coordinating directly with district teams and local NGOs who are the ones actually turning a plan into a working latrine, a functioning water point, or a classroom that stays open.

The part of this role that has shaped me most is donor reporting — not because it's exciting, but because it's a test of integrity that repeats every single cycle. Donors are trusting me with resources meant for children and communities who will never see the spreadsheet, and I've made it a personal standard that every report I file is accurate enough that it could survive any level of scrutiny. That discipline is what keeps a small NGO's word worth something over six years and counting.

What I've come to understand doing this work part-time, alongside everything else, is that community development isn't a campaign — it's a maintenance commitment. There's no summit-style finish line where the sanitation project is “done.” There's only the ongoing question of whether the system installed two years ago still works today, and whether the school that got new water access last year still has it. Staying in this role since 2019 has taught me the patience that every other part of my work depends on.

- Oversee education, sanitation, and community-development activities across 18 districts and 29 schools
- Coordinate directly with district teams and local NGOs to keep field-level delivery on track
- Maintain rigorous stakeholder and donor reporting to protect financial transparency and trust
- Lead monitoring & evaluation to ensure long-term project outcomes, not just short-term completion

### Trainer (Consultant) — Connection Nepal (2019 to Present)
You can't teach disaster preparedness from a slide deck, and you can't teach menstrual hygiene to a room that doesn't trust you yet. I learned that in my very first sessions as a Trainer with Connection Nepal, and it shaped everything about how I've approached this role since. Designing a national training program is the easy part — the real work is standing in front of a classroom of skeptical teenagers, or a circle of community elders, and earning enough trust in one session that they'll actually change a behavior after you leave.

Over the years, that work has taken me across more than 10 districts, training over 5,000 youth, educators, and community members on Disaster Risk Reduction, Climate Change Adaptation, Menstrual Hygiene Management, and WASH. Each topic comes with its own resistance to push through — DRR competes with the belief that disasters are unpredictable and unavoidable; MHM competes with silence and stigma; climate adaptation competes with the sense that the problem is too big for any one village to act on. My job isn't just to deliver information. It's to dismantle the reason people have for not acting on it yet.

What keeps me returning to the same districts year after year is simple: a single training session changes very little. A relationship, sustained over multiple visits, changes behavior for good. I don't just deliver a curriculum and leave — I build the training manuals, the partnership proposals, and the follow-up relationships that make sure the knowledge doesn't fade the week after I'm gone. This is the quietest work I do, and also the one I'm most certain matters.

- Designed and delivered national training programs on DRR, Climate Change Adaptation, MHM, and WASH
- Trained 5,000+ youth, educators, and community members across 10+ districts
- Built sustained, in-person trust that turned single sessions into lasting behavior change
- Developed training manuals and partnership proposals with local and international stakeholders

### SAP Coordinator — Rotaract Club of Sukedhara (Jun 2019 to Dec 2020)
Every long career has a first small task that nobody remembers except the person who did it. Mine was coordinating service projects for a single club — chasing down volunteers, confirming venues, following up with partners who'd said yes weeks earlier and then gone quiet. Nothing about it was glamorous, and that was exactly the point. I learned that a "project" isn't an idea, it's a checklist someone actually finishes, and that stakeholders don't remember your good intentions — they remember whether you called back when you said you would.

That habit of following through became the foundation for every larger role that came after. Long before I coordinated national summits, I was learning the same lesson at club scale: consistency is the only currency that builds trust.

- Coordinated grassroots service projects from planning through execution
- Managed stakeholder engagement and follow-through at the club level
- Built the habits of reliability and consistency that carried into every later role

### President — Rotaract Club of Sukedhara (Jul 2020 to Jun 2021)
A year in, the club handed me something heavier than a task list — accountability for the whole thing. As President, I led club operations and community service initiatives during one of the hardest stretches for youth organizations anywhere: the middle of a global disruption, when in-person service was harder to organize and members were easier to lose. I had to rethink how a club stays active when the usual playbook doesn't apply, keeping morale up and service moving even when circumstances were working against us.

This was my first real lesson in ownership. When a member's experience was good, that was a team effort. When something fell through, that was on me to fix — not to explain away. I left the role having learned that leadership is measured less by the plans you make and more by what you do when the plan breaks.

- Directed full club operations and community-service programming for a full term
- Sustained member engagement and service delivery through a difficult operating period
- Took first full ownership of outcomes rather than individual tasks

### Secretary — Amnesty International Tri-Chandra Youth Network (Jan 2020 to Aug 2022)
Parallel to my Rotaract path, I was learning a different discipline entirely: advocacy without applause. As Secretary of the Amnesty International Tri-Chandra Youth Network, I supported human rights awareness and advocacy initiatives — work where the audience is often small, the topics are uncomfortable, and progress is measured in years, not event cycles.

This role sharpened something that shows up in everything I do now: the ability to talk about difficult, sometimes unpopular subjects clearly and respectfully, and to keep showing up for a cause even when it isn't the easiest room to be in. It's the same discipline I now bring to training sessions on sensitive topics like menstrual hygiene and climate risk — the comfort with hard conversations was built here first.

- Supported human rights education and advocacy campaigns over a two-and-a-half-year term
- Developed comfort engaging communities on sensitive, high-stakes topics
- Built long-view patience for causes with slow, incremental progress

### Immediate Past President — Rotaract Club of Sukedhara (Jul 2021 to Jun 2022)
Stepping down from President didn't mean stepping away. As Immediate Past President, I provided advisory support for leadership continuity and club growth — sitting beside the new leadership team, answering the questions I once had no one to ask, and making sure institutional knowledge didn't walk out the door with my term.

It's easy to think leadership ends when the title does. This role taught me the opposite: the real test of whether you built something lasting is whether it's still standing, and still improving, after you've handed it off. That question has followed me into every role since — I don't just want to lead well, I want what I build to outlast my involvement in it.

- Provided structured advisory support during a full leadership transition
- Preserved institutional knowledge and continuity for incoming club leadership
- Reinforced a personal standard: build things that outlast your own tenure

### Member — T.U. SEG Student Chapter (Society of Exploration Geophysicists) (Jul 2021 to Present)
Leadership development doesn't happen on only one track, and I've made a point of keeping an academic and technical thread running alongside my community work. As a member of the T.U. SEG Student Chapter, I've taken part in academic and leadership activities within a scientific community — a very different environment from a youth-development summit, but one that sharpens the same underlying skill: thinking rigorously, communicating technical ideas clearly, and contributing meaningfully to a group with its own standards and culture.

This ongoing involvement is a reminder to myself as much as anyone else that well-rounded leadership draws from more than one discipline. The precision I've picked up here shows up quietly in how I structure reports, evaluate program outcomes, and hold myself to evidence rather than assumption.

- Sustained multi-year engagement in an academic and scientific student community
- Contributed to leadership and organizational activities outside the nonprofit/youth-development space
- Strengthened analytical rigor now applied to program monitoring and evaluation

### Sergeant-at-Arms — Rotaract District 3292 (Jul 2022 to Jun 2023)
Moving to the district level for the first time, I took on a role most people never think twice about — Sergeant-at-Arms. I supported meeting protocols and district event coordination, the invisible scaffolding that keeps a room full of club leaders from two countries running on time, on agenda, and on the same page.

It would have been easy to treat this as a minor role. Instead, I treated it as an apprenticeship in scale: this was my first close look at how a 150-club district actually functions day to day, long before I'd be asked to help lead it. Structure, I learned here, isn't bureaucracy — it's what lets a large, diverse group actually get things done together.

- Managed meeting protocol and order for district-level proceedings
- Coordinated logistics for multi-club district events
- Gained early, close-up exposure to district-scale operations ahead of later leadership roles

### Goodwill Ambassador — The Asha Project Nepal (Jan 2022 to Present)
This role has quietly run underneath almost everything else I've done since 2022. As Goodwill Ambassador for The Asha Project Nepal, I advocate for youth empowerment and social-impact initiatives wherever I go — in district meetings, training halls, and now on national summit stages. It isn't a scheduled responsibility with fixed hours; it's a lens I carry into every other role.

What this ambassadorship has given me is a consistent "why" underneath a resume that could otherwise look scattered across nonprofits, districts, and a business institute. Every version of the work — sanitation projects, entrepreneurship summits, Rotaract mentorship — traces back to the same conviction: that young people do extraordinary things when someone invests in them early and consistently.

- Champion youth empowerment and social-impact messaging across multiple platforms and audiences
- Provide a consistent advocacy thread connecting grassroots, district, and national-level work
- Represent Asha Project Nepal's mission in public and institutional settings

### Assistant District Secretary — Rotaract District 3292 (2023 to 2024)
Back at the district level in a more demanding capacity, I managed district records, reporting, and communication between clubs and the district council. This is the kind of role where success is invisible — nobody praises you for a report that was accurate and on time, but everyone notices if it isn't. I made sure the flow of information between more than a hundred clubs and the district leadership never broke down.

This role became the operational backbone for everything I'd do at the district level afterward. When I later stepped into representative and secretary roles, I already understood exactly how information, requests, and decisions were supposed to move through the system — because I'd spent a year making sure they did.

- Maintained accurate district records and reporting systems
- Managed two-way communication flow between clubs and the district council
- Built the operational foundation later used in district representative and secretary roles

### Club Adviser — Rotaract Club of Sukedhara (Jul 2023 to Present)
I came back to where it all started, this time as a mentor instead of a member. As Club Adviser, I guide the current leadership team in strategy, project planning, and execution — the same three things I once had to learn from scratch as SAP Coordinator and President. Now I'm the person a nervous new president can call before a big decision, the way I once wished someone was for me.

There's a particular kind of satisfaction in watching a club you once led make decisions you never would have thought of — and realizing your job now is to support that, not to control it. This role keeps me honest about what good mentorship actually looks like: guidance offered, not control imposed.

- Advise current club leadership on strategy, planning, and project execution
- Transfer institutional knowledge from a full presidency term to the next generation
- Model hands-off, empowerment-based mentorship rather than directive leadership

### Program Officer — Nepal Business Institute (Oct 2024 to Sep 2025)
This is where everything converged. Every skill built across five years of club and district leadership — outreach, coordination, follow-through, comfort with difficult conversations — suddenly had a national stage to operate on. As Program Officer, I helped coordinate two of the country's largest youth and business gatherings, the Nepal Business Summit 2025 and the Youth Entrepreneurship Summit 2025, engaging colleges and youth networks across the entire country.

The scale was new, but the fundamentals weren't. I ran targeted outreach campaigns and had the same kind of one-on-one conversations I'd been having since 2019, just now with national sponsors, media contacts, and policymakers instead of club members. I documented what worked after each event, the same discipline I'd learned keeping district records years earlier, and used it to make the next summit stronger.

- Coordinated execution of two flagship national events: Nepal Business Summit 2025 and Youth Entrepreneurship Summit 2025
- Drove participant recruitment through digital campaigns and direct, one-to-one outreach
- Built sponsor, media, and policymaker relationships to expand national visibility
- Documented outcomes to directly inform the following year's strategy

### Assistant District Rotaract Representative — Rotaract District 3292 (2024 to 2025)
At the same time my national career was accelerating, my role in Rotaract deepened into something more people-focused than any I'd held before. As Assistant District Rotaract Representative, I mentored club presidents and secretaries across the district on project planning, member retention, and leadership growth — essentially becoming, for dozens of young leaders, the adviser I'd once needed myself.

I also coordinated national training seminars like RYTS and DRR Installation, and supported service campaigns that turned that training into visible community action. This was the year the throughline of my whole career became unmistakable to me: whether it's a Rotaract club president or a first-time summit attendee, my real job is finding people with potential and staying close enough, long enough, to help it become real.

- Mentored dozens of club presidents and secretaries across the district
- Coordinated national training seminars, including RYTS and DRR Installation
- Supported service campaigns translating training into direct community impact
- Strengthened member retention and leadership pipelines district-wide

### District Secretary — Rotaract District 3292 (2025 to 2026)
Today, at the district level, I lead administration, communications, and strategic planning for more than 150 Rotaract clubs spanning two countries — Nepal and Bhutan. Every committee, every project, every district initiative is aligned to Rotary's Areas of Focus and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, so that grassroots service work connects to something larger than any single club.

What strikes me most, holding this role, is the direct line back to 2019: the same instincts that made me double-check a volunteer list for one club now scale into coordinating strategic alignment across an entire binational network. The scope changed completely. The underlying discipline never did.

- Lead district administration, communications, and strategic planning for 150+ clubs
- Oversee a binational network spanning Nepal and Bhutan
- Align grassroots club projects with Rotary's Areas of Focus and the UN SDGs
- Coordinate district committees to maintain strategic consistency at scale

### Program Manager — Nepal Business Institute (Sep 2025 to Present)
This is the role every earlier one was quietly building toward. As Program Manager, I lead the planning and execution of Nepal's flagship business and entrepreneurship summits — owning strategy, sponsorship, government liaison, budgeting, and the complete participant journey from the first outreach message to post-event follow-up, months later.

What makes this role different from every one before it isn't the size of the stage. It's that nothing here is new to me — the outreach reflects lessons from 2019, the stakeholder coordination reflects district-level discipline, the mentorship instincts reflect years of advising club leaders, and the advocacy reflects a Goodwill Ambassador role I've carried since 2022. Six years of separate roles didn't just happen alongside each other. They were training for this one.

- Own end-to-end strategy, budgeting, and delivery for national-level summits
- Direct outreach and cultivation with colleges, youth networks, sponsors, and government stakeholders
- Manage the complete participant experience from first contact through post-program follow-up
- Lead team coordination and reporting to consistently meet or exceed program goals

## Frequently asked questions
### Who is Chandra Bhakta Adhikari?
Chandra Bhakta Adhikari is a Nepal-based Program Manager and Strategic Partnerships professional working across youth leadership, entrepreneurship, stakeholder engagement and community development. He has 5+ years of experience with NGOs, government and business, is based in Bhaktapur, and is a geologist by training (B.Sc., Tribhuvan University).

### What is Chandra Bhakta Adhikari's current role?
He is Program Manager at Nepal Business Institute, where he leads planning and execution of national business and youth-entrepreneurship summits such as the Nepal Business Summit. He joined the institute as Program Officer in October 2024. He also serves as Project Coordinator at Asha Project Nepal and as a training consultant with Connection Nepal.

### What is the Nepal Business Summit and what does he do there?
The Nepal Business Summit is a national program run by Nepal Business Institute that brings together ministries, sponsors, media and entrepreneurs. Chandra coordinated the 2025 Nepal Business Summit and Nepal Youth Entrepreneurship Summit as Program Officer, and now leads the program as Program Manager, covering strategy, budget, sponsorship, government liaison, stall allocation and media.

### What training does Chandra Bhakta Adhikari deliver?
Since 2019 he has been a trainer and consultant with Connection Nepal, delivering Disaster Risk Reduction, Climate Change Adaptation, Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) and WASH training. He has trained 5,000+ youth, educators and community members, including in rural municipalities such as Baitadi, Rautahat, Sindhupalchok and Mahottari.

### What is his role in Rotaract District 3292?
Chandra served as District Secretary of Rotaract District 3292 (Nepal & Bhutan) for 2025–26, handling communication, governance and records for 150+ clubs. Since 2019 he has progressed through SAP Coordinator, Club President, Immediate Past President, Sergeant-at-Arms, Assistant District Secretary and Assistant District Rotaract Representative, and is Adviser to the Rotaract Club of Sukedhara.

### What does Asha Project Nepal do, and what is his part in it?
Chandra has been Project Coordinator at Asha Project Nepal since January 2019, overseeing education, sanitation and community-development activities across 18 districts and 29 schools. His work includes coordinating with district teams and local NGOs, donor reporting and monitoring & evaluation. He is also the organization's Goodwill Ambassador.

### Where is Chandra Bhakta Adhikari based, and what is his educational background?
He is based in Bhaktapur, Nepal, and was born in Phidim, Panchthar. He holds a B.Sc. in Geology from Tribhuvan University, with field experience in GIS, mapping, ERT and SRT surveys. He speaks Nepali, English and Hindi.

### What certifications does he hold?
He holds 21 professional certifications earned between January and June 2025, covering project management, event management, leadership, public speaking, HR strategy, GIS, internet marketing and cloud fundamentals. They were issued by Udemy, MTF Institute, Oxford Home Study Center, eLearning College and Simplilearn, and each is listed with its credential ID on the Experience page.

### Has Chandra Bhakta Adhikari received any awards?
Yes. He received Outstanding Rotaract Project (2019–20) and Outstanding Rotaract District Member (2022–23 and 2023–24), both from Rotary International District 3292.

### Is he available for speaking, training or partnerships?
Yes. He is open to speaking invitations, training requests and strategic partnerships, including keynotes, panels and facilitation on youth leadership, entrepreneurship, MHM/WASH and disaster risk reduction. Reach him at hello@adhikarichandra.com.np or through the Contact page.

### What does Chandra Adhikari do?
Chandra Adhikari (Chandra Bhakta Adhikari) is a Program Manager and Strategic Partnerships professional in Nepal. He plans and delivers national youth-entrepreneurship programs at Nepal Business Institute, builds partnerships with colleges, NGOs, sponsors and government stakeholders, and trains communities in MHM, WASH and Disaster Risk Reduction.

### What is Chandra Bhakta Adhikari known for?
He is known in Nepal for organizing national business and youth-entrepreneurship summits, for leadership in Rotaract District 3292 (Nepal & Bhutan, 150+ clubs), and for MHM, WASH and Disaster Risk Reduction training that has reached 5,000+ youth, educators and community members.

### Where does Chandra Bhakta Adhikari work?
He works as Program Manager at Nepal Business Institute (NBI), as Project Coordinator at The Asha Project Nepal, and as a Trainer (Consultant) with Connection Nepal. He is based in Bhaktapur, in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.

### What is Chandra Adhikari's role at NBI and in NYES?
NBI is Nepal Business Institute and NYES is the Nepal Youth Entrepreneurship Summit. Chandra coordinated the 2025 Nepal Business Summit and the 2025 NYES as Program Officer, and now leads planning and delivery of NBI's national youth-entrepreneurship programs as Program Manager, including sponsorship, government liaison, media and stakeholder coordination.

### What organizations is Chandra Bhakta Adhikari associated with?
Nepal Business Institute (Program Manager), The Asha Project Nepal (Project Coordinator and Goodwill Ambassador), Connection Nepal (Trainer and Consultant), Rotaract District 3292 (District Secretary 2025–26), the Rotaract Club of Sukedhara (Club Adviser), the T.U. SEG Student Chapter (Member) and, formerly, Amnesty International's Tri-Chandra Youth Network.

### What are Chandra Adhikari's professional interests?
His professional interests are youth leadership, entrepreneurship development, strategic partnerships, stakeholder engagement, event and summit management, community development, Menstrual Hygiene Management, WASH, Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, and GIS and geology from his academic background.

### Are Chandra Adhikari, Bhakta Adhikari and C.B. Adhikari the same person?
On this website, yes: Chandra Bhakta Adhikari is also written Chandra Adhikari, Bhakta Adhikari, Chandra B. Adhikari and C.B. Adhikari. Adhikari is a common surname in Nepal, so to identify him look for Nepal Business Institute, Rotaract District 3292, Connection Nepal or The Asha Project Nepal, and a base in Bhaktapur.
